expectedText:
QUALIFIED SMALL BUSINESS STOCK (QSBS) GAIN EXCLUSION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Innovations, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes how federal and California law treat gain from the sale or exchange of stock that may qualify as "qualified small business stock" under Internal Revenue Code section 1202 -- a federal tax category most often discussed in connection with early stock issued by a venture-stage C corporation such as Acme Innovations, Inc. It states facts about the federal exclusion regime, about a 2025 federal statutory amendment to that regime, and about California's separate, non-conforming income tax treatment of the same gain. It does not determine whether any stock actually held by Jordan Lee in Acme Innovations, Inc. meets the federal statute's requirements, does not calculate any excludable or taxable amount, and does not complete a federal or California tax return or other filing.

FEDERAL LAW: WHAT COUNTS AS "QUALIFIED SMALL BUSINESS STOCK"
Under federal law, stock must meet threshold conditions before it can be treated as "qualified small business stock" at all. It must be stock in a C corporation, acquired by the holder at original issue rather than purchased later from another shareholder, issued by a corporation that meets a statutory ceiling on "aggregate gross assets" -- currently $75,000,000 -- measured both before and immediately after the stock's issuance. Whether stock issued by Acme Innovations, Inc. to Jordan Lee satisfies either condition depends on facts about how and when that stock was acquired and what Acme Innovations, Inc.'s aggregate gross assets were at the relevant times; this document does not establish those facts for any specific stock.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Except as otherwise provided in this section, the term “qualified small business stock” means any stock in a C corporation which is originally issued after the date of the enactment of the Revenue Reconciliation Act of 1993, if—"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202(c)(1) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, the original-issue and C-corporation conditions for "qualified small business stock" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  "the aggregate gross assets of such corporation (or any predecessor thereof) at all times on or after the date of the enactment of the Revenue Reconciliation Act of 1993 and before the issuance did not exceed $75,000,000,"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202(d)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, the $75,000,000 aggregate-gross-assets ceiling for a "qualified small business" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  Known gap: Both citations are drawn from law.cornell.edu's Legal Information Institute (LII), an unofficial but widely used mirror of the U.S. Code sourced from the Office of the Law Revision Counsel; this clause was not independently cross-checked against the official text on govinfo.gov. The $75,000,000 gross-assets figure quoted here reflects the amount as amended in 2025 (see the separate clause on the 2025 amendment elsewhere in this document) -- a source using an older reference (including many pre-2026 secondary summaries) may still state the prior $50,000,000 figure. This clause states only the gross-assets and original-issue conditions; it does not address the several other conditions the statute separately imposes (the active business requirement, the anti-redemption rules, and others), which are addressed, where covered at all, in separate clauses of this document.

FEDERAL LAW: THE ACTIVE BUSINESS REQUIREMENT
Separately from the original-issue and gross-assets conditions, federal law requires that -- during substantially all of the holder's holding period -- the issuing corporation actually meet an "active business" requirement and remain a C corporation. Stock in a corporation that does not meet this ongoing requirement is not qualified small business stock, regardless of how or when it was originally issued.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Stock in a corporation shall not be treated as qualified small business stock unless, during substantially all of the taxpayer’s holding period for such stock, such corporation meets the active business requirements of subsection (e) and such corporation is a C corporation."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202(c)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, the ongoing active-business and C-corporation-status requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  Known gap: The "active business requirements of subsection (e)" cross-referenced here include a lengthy, separately defined list -- among other things, subsection (e) excludes certain service, banking, financing, farming, hotel, restaurant, and mineral-extraction businesses from counting as an active qualified trade or business, and imposes further asset-composition tests. This clause quotes only the general cross-reference to subsection (e); it does not itself quote or describe that subsection's itemized list of disqualifying business types, and does not determine whether a specific corporation's actual business activities would satisfy or fail that list at any given time.

FEDERAL LAW: HOW MUCH GAIN CAN BE EXCLUDED, AND FOR HOW LONG THE STOCK MUST BE HELD
Federal law excludes a portion of gain from a qualifying sale from a noncorporate taxpayer's gross income, but the portion excluded and the required holding period depend on when the stock was acquired relative to a statutory dividing line the statute calls the "applicable date." For stock acquired on or before the applicable date, the general rule excludes 50 percent of the gain, and only after the stock has been held for more than five years. For stock acquired after the applicable date, a different, tiered rule applies instead, keyed to a shorter minimum holding period of at least three years.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "except as provided in paragraphs (3) and (4), 50 percent of any gain from the sale or exchange of qualified small business stock acquired on or before the applicable date and held for more than 5 years, and"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, the 50 percent exclusion and five-year holding period for stock acquired on or before the applicable date (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  "the applicable percentage of any gain from the sale or exchange of qualified small business stock acquired after the applicable date and held for at least 3 years."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202(a)(1)(B) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, the tiered exclusion and three-year minimum holding period for stock acquired after the applicable date (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  Known gap: The pre-applicable-date 50 percent figure quoted here is itself qualified by "except as provided in paragraphs (3) and (4)" -- separate statutory provisions that substitute 75 percent or 100 percent exclusion rates for stock acquired within specific windows in 2009 and 2010 forward. This clause does not restate those separate provisions or their date windows, and does not determine which acquisition-date-specific rate, if any, would apply to any particular block of stock -- that depends on the actual date particular shares were issued, a fact not established here. Separately, the tiered post-applicable-date percentages themselves (50 percent at three years, 75 percent at four years, 100 percent at five years or more) appear in the statute's own table format in the underlying source and are not quoted verbatim in this clause because of how that table renders as plain text once HTML formatting is stripped from the source page; the applicable holding-period floor of "at least 3 years" is quoted directly from the statutory text rather than from the table.

FEDERAL LAW: THE 2025 AMENDMENT AND ITS "APPLICABLE DATE"
The dividing line the statute calls the "applicable date" -- the date that determines which exclusion percentage, holding period, and per-issuer dollar cap apply to a given block of stock -- is itself defined by the statute only by cross-reference to the date a particular federal law was enacted. That enactment was Public Law 119-21, approved July 4, 2025, which amended several parts of this statute, including the exclusion-percentage and per-issuer-cap provisions described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The term “applicable date” means the date of the enactment of this paragraph."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202(a)(6)(A) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, the statutory definition of "applicable date" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  "The date of the enactment of this paragraph, referred to in subsec. (a)(6)(A), is the date of enactment of Pub. L. 119–21, which was approved July 4, 2025."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202, Editorial Notes -- References in Text (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code editorial note identifying July 4, 2025 (enactment of Pub. L. 119-21) as the "applicable date" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  Known gap: This dividing line was enacted on July 4, 2025 -- new enough, as of this document's 2026 preparation date, that no reported court decision interpreting how the amended two-tier regime applies in practice was located; no case-law search specific to this 2025 amendment returned any results to review. The statutory text of subsection (a)(6)(A) is circular on its own (it defines "applicable date" only as "the date of the enactment of this paragraph"); the actual calendar date is supplied not by the codified statutory text itself but by an editorial note accompanying the U.S. Code text -- an official annotation prepared by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel, but not itself enacted, codified law.

FEDERAL LAW: THE PER-ISSUER DOLLAR CAP ON EXCLUDABLE GAIN
Even where stock otherwise qualifies, federal law caps how much gain from any one issuing corporation's stock a taxpayer can exclude over time. For stock acquired on or before the applicable date, the cap is $10,000,000 (reduced by amounts already excluded in prior years for that issuer's stock). For stock acquired after the applicable date, a separate, higher $15,000,000 cap applies instead, reduced by a similarly defined set of prior amounts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "if such stock was acquired by the taxpayer on or before the applicable date, $10,000,000, reduced by the aggregate amount of eligible gain taken into account by the taxpayer under subsection (a) for prior taxable years and attributable to dispositions of stock issued by such corporation and acquired by the taxpayer before, on, or after the applicable date, and"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202(b)(4)(A) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, the $10,000,000 per-issuer cap for stock acquired on or before the applicable date (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  "if such stock was acquired by the taxpayer after the applicable date, $15,000,000, reduced by the sum of—"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 1202(b)(4)(B) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, the $15,000,000 per-issuer cap for stock acquired after the applicable date (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1202)
  Known gap: This clause describes only the two headline dollar figures; it does not restate the alternative "10 times adjusted basis" measure that applies instead whenever it produces a larger allowable amount, and it does not restate the separate married-filing-separately allocation rules. The $15,000,000 post-applicable-date figure is also subject to an inflation adjustment for taxable years beginning after 2026 under a separate paragraph not quoted in this clause; this document does not calculate any inflation-adjusted dollar figure for any specific future taxable year.

CALIFORNIA LAW: NO CURRENT STATE-LEVEL EXCLUSION
California once had its own state income tax exclusion for gain from qualified small business stock, formerly codified at Revenue and Taxation Code section 18152.5, separate from and narrower than the federal exclusion described elsewhere in this document. Legislation enacted in 2013 limited that state exclusion's operation to sales occurring in taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2008 and before January 1, 2013, and set the section itself to sunset -- to remain in effect only until January 1, 2016, after which it is repealed. Consulting the California Legislative Information website for the current text of former section 18152.5 today returns no operative statutory text for that section, consistent with that repeal.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The amendments made to this section by the act adding this subdivision shall apply to sales, including installment sales, occurring in each taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2008, and before January 1, 2013, and installment payments received in taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2008,  for sales of qualified small business stock made in taxable years beginning before January 1, 2013."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 18152.5(m), as amended by Stats. 2013, ch. 546 (Sen. Bill 209) (California Legislative Information text), 2013 session law limiting the state exclusion's operation to sales in taxable years 2008 through 2012 (https://www.leginfo.ca.gov/pub/13-14/bill/sen/sb_0201-0250/sb_209_bill_20131004_chaptered.htm)
  "This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2016, and as of that date is repealed, unless a later enacted statute, that is enacted before January 1, 2016, deletes or extends that date."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 18152.5(n), as amended by Stats. 2013, ch. 546 (Sen. Bill 209) (California Legislative Information text), 2013 session law sunsetting and repealing the state exclusion section as of January 1, 2016 (https://www.leginfo.ca.gov/pub/13-14/bill/sen/sb_0201-0250/sb_209_bill_20131004_chaptered.htm)
  Known gap: Both citations in this clause come from the same 2013 session-law bill (Senate Bill 209) amending the same statute, so they corroborate one document's history rather than confirming it from independent sources. This document's own attempt to look up the current text of former Revenue and Taxation Code section 18152.5 on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, performed twice with distinct User-Agent strings, returned an empty results page both times -- consistent with, but not itself an authoritative confirmation of, full repeal; an empty page is not a quotable source, so this clause's operative quotes are instead drawn from the 2013 repealing legislation itself. This document does not independently verify that no California legislation enacted after 2013 has reinstated a state-level exclusion for qualified small business stock gain -- it relies on the 2013 sunset provision quoted here and did not perform a fresh line-by-line search of the entire current Revenue and Taxation Code. This clause also addresses only the personal income tax treatment of an individual seller's gain; it does not address California corporate-level tax treatment.

CALIFORNIA LAW: WHY THE FORMER STATE EXCLUSION WAS NARROWED
Before its 2013 amendment and eventual repeal, California's state-level qualified-small-business-stock provisions defined a "qualified small business" in a way that reached only corporations with at least 80 percent of their assets and payroll located in California -- a geographic condition with no counterpart in the federal statute. A California Court of Appeal held that an in-state property-and-payroll requirement of this kind, as applied to a related deferral provision built on the same definition, discriminated on its face against interstate commerce and violated the commerce clause of the U.S. Constitution, reversing a trial court judgment that had upheld the requirement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "classification as a qualified small business requires that “[a]t least 80 percent (by value) of the assets of the corporation [must be] used by the corporation in the active conduct of one or more qualified trades or businesses in California” (§ 18152.5, subd. (e)(1)(A)), and a corporation does not meet this requirement “for any period during which more than 20 percent of the corporation’s total payroll expense is attributable to employment located outside of California” (id., subd. (e)(9))."
  — Cutler v. Franchise Tax Board, 208 Cal. App. 4th 1247 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811291/cutler-v-franchise-tax-board/)
  "because the statute affords taxpayers a deferral for income received from the sale of stock in corporations maintaining assets and payroll in California, while no deferral is afforded for income from the sale of stock in corporations that maintain assets and payroll elsewhere, the deferral provision discriminates on its face on the basis of an interstate element in violation of the commerce clause. We therefore reverse the judgment."
  — Cutler v. Franchise Tax Board, 208 Cal. App. 4th 1247 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811291/cutler-v-franchise-tax-board/)
  "The judgment is reversed and the cause is remanded to the trial court for further proceedings. Plaintiff shall recover his costs on appeal."
  — Cutler v. Franchise Tax Board, 208 Cal. App. 4th 1247 (2012) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5811291/cutler-v-franchise-tax-board/)
  Known gap: The case discussed here, Cutler v. Franchise Tax Board, addressed a stock-sale gain deferral provision (former Revenue and Taxation Code section 18038.5) that incorporated the same California-asset-and-payroll "qualified small business" definition used by the separate gain exclusion provision (former section 18152.5(a)) -- but the opinion's holding is stated in terms of the deferral provision before it, and this document did not find language in the opinion applying its holding to the exclusion provision by name. This document infers the two provisions shared the same constitutionally infirm definitional mechanism from the text of the statute itself, not from an express statement to that effect in the opinion. This is a California Court of Appeal (Second District) decision, not a California Supreme Court decision; the case-law search performed for this document did not locate a California Supreme Court decision reviewing it. It is offered here as background on why California's approach to this topic changed, not as a statement of current operative law -- the current operative fact is the 2013 repeal described in the companion clause of this document.

PREPARATION ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding Acme Innovations, Inc. and stock held by Jordan Lee was completed by Jordan T. Reyes on September 8, 2026 in Oakland, California. It reflects the federal and California statutory and case-law sources cited above as of the date each clause was checked, and it does not itself determine tax treatment for any specific sale or exchange of stock.
